query: Consider a eutectic high-entropy alloy (HEA) composed of FCC and ordered B2 phases. The operating regime involves intermediate thermal aging where classical grain-boundary embrittlement is absent. Known failure involves a dramatic, transient loss of ductility (brittleness) at specific aging temperatures, followed by recovery at higher temperatures. Design constraints require that the mechanism must account for the evolution of local chemical orders (LCOs) and phase boundary (PB) morphologies rather than impurity segregation or grain coarsening. Propose a hypothesis linking the evolution of LCOs and PBs to the observed ductile-brittle-ductile transition. What prior evidence regarding dislocation behavior in ordered domains supports this? Define the specific boundary of the embrittlement regime and a discriminating measurement to falsify the grain-boundary mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: The evolution of local chemical orders (LCOs) and phase boundary (PB) morphologies in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (HEA) composed of FCC and ordered B2 phases leads to a dramatic, transient loss of ductility (brittleness) at specific aging temperatures, followed by recovery at higher temperatures, due to the interaction between dislocations and the LCOs/PBs.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (HEA) composed of FCC and ordered B2 phases
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical orders (LCOs) and phase boundary (PB) morphologies
generation.mechanism: Interaction between dislocations and the LCOs/PBs
generation.predicted_outcome: Transient loss of ductility (brittleness) at specific aging temperatures, followed by recovery at higher temperatures
generation.boundary: Specific aging temperatures where embrittlement occurs
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of interaction between dislocations and LCOs/PBs is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Thermal aging experiments at various temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no correlation is found between LCOs/PBs and ductility loss, the hypothesis is falsified

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
